hints: Look closely at the carbon that carries the chlorine and count how many other carbons are attached to it.
1-chloro-2-methylbutane is $\text{CH}_2\text{ClCH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, so the $\text{C-Cl}$ carbon is primary with two H atoms and one alkyl group.
Recall how a primary haloalkane reacts with a strong nucleophile like $\text{CN}^-$, and think whether you expect a one-step transition state with partial bonds or a free carbocation.
walkthrough:
**Draw the starting haloalkane**

First, work out the structure. 1-chloro-2-methylbutane is $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl-CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

The carbon bonded to $\text{Cl}$ is bonded to only one other carbon, so it is a primary haloalkane.

**Choose SN1 or SN2**

Primary haloalkanes strongly favour $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ with a good nucleophile like cyanide, $\text{CN}^-$.

$$\text{R-CH}_2\text{-Cl} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{R-CH}_2\text{-CN} + \text{Cl}^-$$
$S_{N}1$ would need a primary carbocation, $\text{R-CH}_2^+$, which is very unstable and does not form readily.

**Describe the SN2 transition state**

$S_{N}2$ is one step with no intermediate. The nucleophile attacks from the back as the leaving group leaves.

The transition state has partial bonds and a negative charge:
$$[\text{NC} \cdots \text{C} \cdots \text{Cl}]^-$$
The central carbon still has its original three groups: two $\text{H}$ atoms and $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. That matches the correct diagram exactly.

options.A: This is the SN2 transition state for a primary substrate. Central carbon shows two H atoms plus CH(CH3)CH2CH3, with partial bonds NC---C---Cl and an overall negative charge. This is exactly expected for backside attack by CN- on CH2Cl.
options.B: This shows an SN2 transition state but on the wrong carbon skeleton, with three alkyl groups around the central carbon. It looks like attack at a tertiary centre, not the primary CH2Cl carbon of 1-chloro-2-methylbutane.
options.C: This is a tertiary carbocation, the SN1 intermediate for a tertiary haloalkane. It would form only if Cl left a tertiary carbon to give (CH3)2C+CH2CH3. Our starting material is primary, so this rearranged skeleton is irrelevant.
options.D: This is a primary carbocation, $\text{R-CH}_2^+$, the SN1 intermediate. Primary carbocations are too unstable to form here, especially with strong nucleophile CN- present. The reaction goes by SN2, not SN1, so no free carbocation appears.
